articles.title: How to choose an accounting recruiter in Vancouver
articles.excerpt: Six questions that separate a recruiter who understands accounting from one who is matching keywords, for firms hiring and for CPAs considering a move.
articles.author: Sharpe Wysman
articles.html:
Vancouver has no shortage of recruitment agencies. Far fewer of them understand the difference between a compilation engagement and a review, or why a candidate who has finished In-Depth Tax Level II is a different hire from one who hasn't. Whether you're a firm hiring or a CPA thinking about your next move, the recruiter you choose shapes who you meet and how much time you spend on the wrong conversations.

1. Have they done the work themselves?

A recruiter who has worked in public practice or industry finance can screen on substance, not keywords. They know which questions reveal real audit-planning experience, and they can tell a candidate honestly what a busy season at a particular firm involves. Ask directly: what is your own background?

2. Do they specialize, or do they recruit for everything?

Generalist agencies cover warehouse staff on Monday and tax managers on Tuesday. A specialist knows the local market: which firms are growing, which teams have turnover, and what a fair offer looks like for a senior manager in Burnaby versus downtown Vancouver.

3. How do they qualify candidates before you see them?

The best recruiters send fewer resumes, not more. Ask how they screen: do they interview every candidate, check designations, and confirm motivation and salary expectations before sending a profile? A shortlist of three well-qualified people is worth more than a pile of fifteen.

4. Will they tell you what you don't want to hear?

If your salary band is below market, or your job description is putting good people off, a good recruiter will say so. For candidates, the same applies: an honest recruiter will tell you when a role isn't right for you, even if it costs them a placement.

5. How do they handle confidentiality?

Many senior searches are confidential on both sides. Your recruiter should never send a resume without the candidate's permission for that specific role, and should be able to explain how they protect a client's identity in the market.

6. What happens after the offer?

Placement isn't the finish line. Ask whether the recruiter stays in touch through onboarding and how they handle a hire that isn't working out. Follow-up is where long-term relationships, and long-term fits, are made.

The short version

Choose a recruiter who understands your profession, is honest when it matters, and measures success by fit rather than volume. That is the standard Sharpe Wysman has worked to since 2008. If you'd like to talk through a role or your own career, get in touch.

articles.title: Moving from public practice to industry: a guide for Vancouver CPAs
articles.excerpt: When to make the move, which roles suit public-practice experience, and how to present your background to an industry employer.
articles.author: Sharpe Wysman
articles.html:
For many CPAs the move from public practice to industry is the biggest career decision after getting their designation. Done at the right time, it opens a path to controller, director of finance and CFO roles. Done too early or too late, it can mean a sideways step. Here's how to think it through.

When is the right time?

There's no single answer, but timing shapes the roles available to you. Candidates who move shortly after designating often step into senior accountant or financial reporting roles. Those who leave as managers or senior managers can compete for controller positions, because they bring experience leading teams, managing deadlines and dealing with clients.

If partnership is a realistic goal at your firm, compare that path honestly with industry. Some firms offer a clear, approved partner track, and that's worth weighing before you leave.

Which industry roles suit public-practice experience?

  • Financial reporting and technical accounting: a natural fit for assurance professionals with ASPE and IFRS depth.
  • Controller: suits managers who have run engagements end to end and can own a month-end close.
  • Tax roles in industry: larger private companies increasingly hire in-house tax specialists, especially those with US exposure.
  • Director of Finance: for senior candidates comfortable with forecasting, systems and commercial decision-making.

How to present your background

Industry hiring managers want to know what you can do for their business, not how many files you reviewed. Translate your experience: instead of "performed audits of private companies", say "assessed controls and financial reporting for manufacturing and distribution clients with revenue up to $50M." Highlight systems you know, teams you've led, and moments where your advice changed a client's decision.

What changes day to day

Expect fewer, deeper relationships instead of many clients, more involvement in decisions, and a different rhythm: month-end and year-end rather than busy season. Some people miss the variety of public practice; many find industry gives them the ownership they were looking for.

Talk it through first

A confidential conversation with a recruiter who has made this transition themselves can save you months. Sharpe Wysman's recruiters are designated accountants, and we're happy to talk through your options with no obligation. Learn how we work with candidates.

articles.title: Partner-track roles: seven questions to ask before you accept
articles.excerpt: "Partner track" can mean anything from an approved business case to a vague promise. Here's how to tell the difference.
articles.author: Sharpe Wysman
articles.html:
Few phrases in accounting recruitment carry as much weight, or as much ambiguity, as "partner track". For a senior manager it can be the most important factor in choosing a firm. Before you accept, make sure you understand exactly what's on offer.

1. Is there an approved business case?

The strongest partner-track roles are backed by a business case the existing partners have already approved. Ask whether one exists and when you'll see the details. If the answer is "we'll see how it goes", treat the role as a senior manager position with possible upside.

2. What is the realistic timeline?

One to three years is common for experienced senior managers. Ask what the timeline depends on, and what would speed it up or slow it down.

3. What are the admission criteria?

Book of business, chargeable hours, practice development, people leadership? Get the criteria in writing so both sides measure the same things.

4. What does buy-in look like?

Understand the capital contribution, how it's financed, and how partner income is allocated. A good firm will explain this openly once you're in serious discussions.

5. Who has made partner recently?

Ask how many internal and external candidates have been admitted in the last five years. A firm that regularly promotes partners has a working process. One that hasn't in a decade may not.

6. Will you have real autonomy?

Partnership should mean ownership: a say in strategy, hiring and the clients you take on. Ask current partners how decisions are actually made.

7. What's the work-life balance at partner level?

Some firms keep partners to around 200 hours of overtime a year. Others expect far more. Ask partners directly, and ask what busy season looks like for them.

Get an informed second opinion

We regularly recruit for genuine partner-track roles across Greater Vancouver, including positions with approved business cases. If you're weighing an offer, or wondering whether your current firm's path is real, we're happy to talk it through confidentially.
